title: The Robot That Was Picked Up: A Cloud That Is Sure and Wrong, the Fall in How Well It Explains the Scan, and Scattering a Few New Guesses Until One Is Right

questions.question: Why does a localiser that has found the robot not notice when the robot is picked up?
options: The lidar is off while it is carried
The map is updated to match
The weights are normalised, so the cloud stays as sure as ever of the wrong place
The odometry keeps it in place
questions.explanation: After normalising, the weights add to one whether the scan fits well or badly. The number that fell is the average likelihood before normalising.

questions.question: A plain cloud after a carry of 5.6 m was out by:
questions.explanation: With no particles anywhere near the new place there is nothing to weigh up. The cloud stayed where it was, sure and wrong.

questions.question: With the monitor the robot was found again after how many steps?
questions.explanation: It was called lost after one step, and scattered particles took 21 steps to land near the truth and take over the cloud.

questions.question: Before the robot was moved the monitor put in how much random?
questions.explanation: While the robot was where the cloud said, the two averages agreed and almost nothing was scattered. The error was 0.006 m with the monitor and without.

questions.question: What does the ratio of the fast to the slow average show?
options: Whether the scans are explained now as well as they usually are
How fast the robot is moving
How old the last resampling is
questions.explanation: The slow average is the usual level of fit and the fast one the recent level. When the fast one drops below the slow one, something has changed.

questions.question: Why is the share of random particles limited?
options: Random particles are expensive to draw
The map has a limited area
One bad scan must not throw a good cloud away
questions.explanation: A person walking past spoils a scan without the robot having moved. Capped at 20 percent, the cloud survives it.
